analysis.one_liner: Bans hiring anyone under 18 to handle tobacco plants or leaves on farms.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate committee it was referred to on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal child labor rules have long treated farm work more loosely than other jobs, allowing 16- and 17-year-olds to work in tobacco fields, where contact with the plant can cause nicotine poisoning. This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to classify any paid work by a person under 18 that involves direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves as illegal "oppressive child labor." The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 18 who work for pay on tobacco farms, and their families, would gain protection from nicotine exposure, long hours in heat, and machinery hazards that currently fall through the agricultural exemptions in federal child labor law. Adults working the same fields would also benefit from a clearer standard and pressure on growers to hire only adults.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act so that any employee under 18 with direct contact with tobacco plants or dried tobacco leaves is counted under the law's "oppressive child labor" prohibition, closing the agricultural carve-out that otherwise lets teens work tobacco [S2].

The change applies to tobacco-related agriculture specifically, the one crop where handling the raw product exposes workers' skin to nicotine absorbed at levels linked to vomiting, dizziness, and other acute symptoms [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco growers who rely on teenage hired labor would lose that workforce and would need to hire adults or restructure harvest work; labor contractors and the tobacco supply chain would absorb some added cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco growers and farm labor contractors

drawbacks.text: Families of farmworkers are low-income, and banning paid tobacco work for under-18s removes one source of income for some of those families during harvest season; the bill contains no income replacement or transition aid [S2].

Opponents of tobacco-specific child labor rules have argued in the past that teens legally can work other hazardous jobs and that a crop-specific ban is arbitrary; the bill would also rely on the Labor Department's existing child labor enforcement, which is thinly staffed in rural areas [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: nicotine absorption through the skin is a documented hazard unique to tobacco harvest, and no other legal job exposes 16- and 17-year-olds to it the way tobacco fields do. The cost falls on a small number of low-income families who lose a seasonal income source, and on growers' labor costs. The bill's main weakness is not its goal but its fate: it never received any committee attention, so no trade-offs were ever weighed in a hearing or amendment.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on June 12, 2023, joined by original cosponsors Senator Brown and Senator Blumenthal [S1][S2][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed [S4].
Three Democratic senators cosponsored the bill in total, and no Republican did; it remained stuck in committee for the rest of the 118th Congress [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco growers and farm labor contractors who depend on teenage harvest labor are better off, since the ban never took effect; child farmworkers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban paid tobacco work for anyone under 18 and referred it to committee.

for.name: Sens. Sherrod Brown and Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Tobacco industry and grower groups
against.role: Tobacco growers and farm labor contractors
against.what_they_did: Opposed crop-specific child labor restrictions on tobacco farms in prior regulatory rounds; no Senate committee ever took the bill up.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the committee that declined to act was chaired by a senator of the other party's majority, so the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Tobacco growers and farm labor contractors
industries.note: The bill would end their legal ability to hire under-18 workers for tobacco harvest, the crop where skin contact with the plant causes nicotine poisoning. Their interest in keeping teen labor available runs against the health protection the bill offers child workers.

Leaf buyers have pushed supply-chain child labor policies abroad and at home; a domestic ban would raise leaf costs and shrink one labor pool, but would also remove a reputational liability. Their position on the bill was not on the congressional record.
